name: Tang Dynasty
summary: A golden age of Chinese culture and power. Its capital Chang’an was one of the largest cities in the world, famous for poetry and trade.

knownFor.label: Woodblock printing
knownFor.note: The Diamond Sutra (868) is the oldest dated printed book.

knownFor.label: Chang’an
knownFor.note: One of the world’s largest cities.

location.value: China proper, ruling from Chang’an (modern Xi’an). At its peak, control reached from northern Vietnam and northern Korea to the Tarim Basin and beyond.

terrain.value: The Guanzhong basin and the North China Plain, linked to the rich Yangtze delta by the Grand Canal. The Hexi Corridor gave access to the Silk Road.

climate.value: Monsoonal. Historians debate whether drier conditions in the 9th century contributed to famine and unrest.
climate.source: Lewis, China’s Cosmopolitan Empire: The Tang Dynasty (2009)

resources.value: Grain from the north and increasingly from the Yangtze south. Salt was so valuable that the salt monopoly provided over half of government revenue by 799.

disasters.value: Grand Canal floods in 858 drowned tens of thousands on the North China Plain. A famine in 873 helped spark the Huang Chao rebellion.

population.value: About 50 million in the 7th century and 80 million in the 9th (Wikipedia infobox). Census counts are debated, especially after the An Lushan rebellion disrupted registration.

urbanisation.value: Chang’an was among the world’s most populous cities, a cosmopolitan capital at the eastern end of the Silk Road. 80–90% of people still lived in the countryside.
urbanisation.source: Wikipedia: Tang dynasty (checked 5 Nov 2026); video research: RESEARCH.md, “5,000 Years of China”

disease.value: No major Tang-era epidemics are described in the sources checked.

migration.value: Population shifted south. The north held about 75% of the population at the start of the dynasty and about 50% at the end. Many foreigners lived in Chang’an and in ports such as Guangzhou and Yangzhou.

economicBase.value: Agriculture under the equal-field land system, which later broke down as large estates grew. Crafts and long-distance trade flourished.

tradeRoutes.value: The overland Silk Road to Central Asia, Persia and beyond. Sea routes from Guangzhou and Yangzhou to Southeast Asia (Srivijaya), India and the Arab world. The Grand Canal internally.

wealth.value: No GDP estimate is given in the sources checked. Its wealth is described in contemporary foreign accounts.

moneyAndTax.value: Bronze cash coins. The Two-Tax reform of 780 replaced grain and labour taxes with semi-annual cash taxes. The salt monopoly became the main revenue source.

inequality.value: Aristocratic clans dominated early on. Large tax-exempt estates grew as the equal-field system collapsed.
inequality.source: Lewis, China’s Cosmopolitan Empire: The Tang Dynasty (2009)

governmentType.value: An imperial monarchy with the Three Departments and Six Ministries. Officials came through examinations (the jinshi degree) and recommendation. The Tang Code (653) had 500 articles.

keyRulers.value: Gaozu (Li Yuan, 618–626). Taizong (626–649). Wu Zetian (ruled as emperor of her own Zhou dynasty, 690–705, China’s only female emperor). Xuanzong (712–756). Ai (904–907, last).
keyRulers.source: Wikipedia: Tang dynasty (checked 5 Nov 2026) (infobox); Britannica: Tang dynasty (checked 8 Nov 2026); World History Encyclopedia: Tang Dynasty (checked 9 Nov 2026)

succession.value: Hereditary, but often violent. Li Shimin (Taizong) killed two brothers in the Xuanwu Gate Incident (626). Coups and poisonings affected the succession in 705–712.

institutions.value: The Tang Code, the examination system, the equal-field system, and military governors (jiedushi) on the frontiers, who became dangerously powerful.

stability.value: The An Lushan Rebellion (755–763) began with over 100,000 troops. The Huang Chao Rebellion (874–884) sacked Chang’an and Luoyang. Medieval sources give very large death tolls, which modern historians dispute.

eliteConflict.value: Eunuchs gained great power at court. The Ganlu Incident (835) failed to remove them. Factional strife among officials, and military governors acting independently after 763.

armyAndTech.value: Professional long-service soldiers replaced rotating conscripts from 737. About 500,000 soldiers by 742. The palace Army of Divine Strategy had 240,000 troops in 798.

majorWars.value: Campaigns in Central Asia (Gaochang 640, Kucha 648). Defeated Goguryeo with Silla (668). The Battle of Talas against the Abbasids (751). The An Lushan Rebellion (755–763). Tibet occupied Chang’an for 15 days in 763.

territoryChange.value: Largest extent around 661–715 (about 5.4 million km² in 715, per the Wikipedia infobox). Lost Central Asia and the Hexi Corridor after 763, partly regained in 848.

alliancesRivals.value: Allied with Silla in Korea. Rivals included the Turkic Khaganates, the Tibetan Empire, the Abbasid Caliphate and Goguryeo. The Uyghurs were allies, then enemies.

inventions.value: Woodblock printing (the Diamond Sutra of 868 is the oldest dated printed book). Gunpowder was discovered by alchemists in the 9th century. Papermaking spread west after Talas.
inventions.source: Wikipedia: Tang dynasty (checked 5 Nov 2026); Wikipedia: Diamond Sutra

scienceEducation.value: State schools and examinations based on the Five Classics. Literacy grew among officials and townspeople. Overall literacy rates are not known.

openness.value: Very open in its early centuries: foreign merchants, envoys and religions (Buddhism, Nestorian Christianity, Manichaeism, Zoroastrianism, Islam) were welcomed. It became more restrictive in the 840s.

communicationTransport.value: A post-station system with horse relays; the Grand Canal; Silk Road and sea routes to the wider world.

religion.value: Buddhism, Taoism and folk religion, with minority faiths of foreign communities. Emperor Wuzong persecuted Buddhism in the 840s.

languageWriting.value: Middle Chinese, and Literary Chinese for government.

artsArchitecture.value: The golden age of Chinese poetry (Li Bai, Du Fu, Wang Wei). Painting (Yan Liben, Zhang Xuan). The Giant Wild Goose Pagoda (652) and the Leshan Giant Buddha (713–803, 71 m).
artsArchitecture.source: Wikipedia: Tang dynasty (checked 5 Nov 2026); video research: RESEARCH.md, “5,000 Years of China”

socialStructure.value: Emperor, aristocratic clans, examination-trained officials, farmers, artisans, merchants, Buddhist clergy, and bonded servants or slaves.
socialStructure.source: Lewis, China’s Cosmopolitan Empire: The Tang Dynasty (2009)

sharedIdentity.value: Called “the people of Tang” (Tangren). The name is still used by Chinese communities abroad.
sharedIdentity.source: Lewis, China’s Cosmopolitan Empire: The Tang Dynasty (2009)

dailyLife.value: Timber houses with tiled roofs; wheat, rice and tea; Chang’an was divided into walled wards locked at night.

neighbours.value: Silla and Japan (which modelled their governments on the Tang), the Tibetan Empire, the Turkic and Uyghur khaganates, the Abbasids, Srivijaya and Champa.

ideasReligions.value: Japanese embassies (ended 894) and monks carried Tang law, Buddhism and city planning to Japan. Envoys came from the Byzantines (643) and Abbasids (758).

colonisation.value: Protectorates in Central Asia, Korea and Vietnam.

riseSignals.value: Inherited the Sui’s reunified state, canal and institutions. Strong early rulers (Taizong), the examination system, and military success in Central Asia.

peakPeriod.value: Early to mid-8th century under Xuanzong, before the An Lushan Rebellion (755–763).
peakPeriod.source: Wikipedia: Tang dynasty (checked 5 Nov 2026); video research: RESEARCH.md, “5,000 Years of China”; Britannica: Tang dynasty (checked 8 Nov 2026); World History Encyclopedia: Tang Dynasty (checked 9 Nov 2026)

declineSignals.value: The An Lushan Rebellion, independent military governors, eunuch power at court, the breakdown of the land system, floods and famine, and the Huang Chao Rebellion (874–884).

outcome.value: Ended in 907 when the warlord Zhu Wen deposed the last emperor and founded the Later Liang. The Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period followed until the Song.
outcome.source: Wikipedia: Tang dynasty (checked 5 Nov 2026); World History Encyclopedia: Tang Dynasty (checked 9 Nov 2026)

sources.value: The Old and New Books of Tang, the Tang Code, Dunhuang manuscripts, and foreign accounts. Checked against Wikipedia on 5 Nov 2026. See also Lewis (2009).

overallCertainty.value: Good for political events. Population figures differ between historians. Medieval death tolls (e.g. for Huang Chao) are disputed. The move to Luoyang is dated 903 or 904 in different parts of the source. Second sources agree: Britannica (checked 8 Nov 2026) gives 618–907, founder Li Yuan (Gaozu) and an apex in the early 8th century; World History Encyclopedia (checked 9 Nov 2026) gives the An Lushan Rebellion as 755–763 and the end in 907 after the warlord Zhu Wen had the last emperors killed.
overallCertainty.source: Wikipedia: Tang dynasty (checked 5 Nov 2026); Britannica: Tang dynasty (checked 8 Nov 2026); World History Encyclopedia: Tang Dynasty (checked 9 Nov 2026)
